implementation_notes: Microsoft.FeatureManagement supplies the router: register with AddFeatureManagement, declare flags in the Microsoft Feature Management schema (a feature_management section in appsettings.json, or Azure App Configuration for runtime updates) and evaluate with IFeatureManager.IsEnabledAsync or gate endpoints, controllers and Razor pages with [FeatureGate]. The libraries' filters are the toggle-context layer - PercentageFilter, TimeWindowFilter and TargetingFilter (which needs WithTargeting and an ITargetingContextAccessor) - and IFeatureManagerSnapshot keeps one request consistent instead of re-evaluating per check. Plain IConfiguration binding of a boolean remains the simpler option for a process-wide flag that needs no targeting.
pitfalls: IsEnabledAsync evaluates per call, so two checks in one request can straddle a flip; use IFeatureManagerSnapshot (or the request-scoped variant manager) when the request must see one consistent state.

Targeting and percentage filters depend on a targeting context: forget WithTargeting (or an ITargetingContextAccessor) and the filter never matches, leaving the flag permanently off instead of failing loudly.
Flags declared in appsettings.json ship with the build while App Configuration flags change underneath it: mixing both makes the effective state of a running system hard to reconstruct.

variants.name: Plain IConfiguration boolean binding
variants.implementation_notes: The library-free realization: any provider of the .NET configuration system (appsettings.json, environment variables, a Key Vault or App Configuration) can act as the flag source, so a section bound into an options object or read through IConfiguration["Features:NewCheckout"] is the whole router. This is the right choice for a handful of process-wide release flags - it needs no additional package and no filter pipeline - and the wrong one once flags must target users, run time windows or be administered by non-developers, which is where the feature-management library starts paying for itself.
pitfalls: A boolean bound from configuration is evaluated on every access of CurrentValue: caching it in a field freezes the flag at construction time, which is rarely what a release toggle wants.
Environment-variable providers cannot express a false override for a key that is absent, so a missing variable silently means "off" - document the default or the flag reads as "not configured".
